items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: US 10Y at 4.8%, Japan 10Y breaks 3% for the first time in three decades — simultaneously
items.idea: US 10-year yield hit 4.795-4.81%, the highest since Trump's return to office. Japan's 10-year broke above 3% for the first time in three decades. Australian and European long yields are rising too, while Brent pushes toward $95. This is a synchronized global sovereign-debt repricing, not a single-country story.
items.angle: Global duration is being sold all at once — this is the 'who pays for AI capex plus fiscal deficits' trade breaking out. Watch long-duration equities and rate-sensitive sectors against this.
items.tweetA: Japan's 10Y just broke 3% for the first time since the early 1990s. US 10Y at 4.8%. Europe's long end climbing too. This isn't a Fed story anymore — it's every G7 sovereign getting repriced at once, and nobody's talking about what that does to the AI capex discount rate.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching Hormuz for the oil headline. The actual story is duration: US, Japan, Australia, Europe all selling long bonds simultaneously. When the whole curve moves together like this, it's not noise — it's the market repricing what governments cost to run.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: China blocked the G20 consensus statement again — and Europe nearly skipped the family photo
items.idea: China refused to support US-backed language calling on surplus countries to reduce distortions suppressing domestic consumption, so there was no formal G20 consensus statement out of Asheville. Separately, European ministers threatened to send deputies rather than pose in the group photo alongside Russia's FM Siluanov.
items.angle: A no-consensus G20 communiqué plus a US-Canada tariff spat (Bessent's submarine joke) signal continued fragmentation of multilateral coordination — supportive of the hard-asset/gold hedge against 'nobody is actually cooperating.'
items.tweetA: No G20 consensus statement. Again. China won't sign language asking surplus countries to boost domestic consumption — the same fight as always, except now it's happening while Japan's yield curve is blowing out. Multilateralism is dead; someone should tell the bond market.
items.tweetB: European finance ministers almost skipped the G20 family photo rather than stand next to Russia's FM. Meanwhile the US and Canada are trading tariff jokes about submarines. This is what 'geopolitical fragmentation' looks like up close — petty theater over a debt-servicing crisis.

items.title: Chamath: don't fund AI silicon startups anymore — the land under the data center is the trade
items.idea: Chamath says land/power ('LPS') is now the fastest path to cash-on-cash returns in AI, and he's acquired ~6GW of grid power and behind-the-meter capacity ramping from today through 2029. He explicitly says he won't invest in AI silicon startups now — chip performance demands, manufacturing precision, and memory supply-chain access make it 'impossible for a startup,' unlike when he helped start Groq (licensed to Nvidia for $20B in Dec 2025) a decade ago.
items.angle: The person who helped launch Groq is now telling people not to fund the next Groq. That's a tell that AI-infra capital has rotated from compute startups to energized land — worth cross-checking against power/utility names.
items.tweetA: The guy who helped start Groq — sold to Nvidia for $20B — just said don't fund AI chip startups anymore. Too capital intensive, memory supply chain locked up. His money now: 6GW of energized land and grid power through 2029. The trade rotated from silicon to real estate.
items.tweetB: Chamath won't touch AI silicon startups anymore but is aggressively buying grid power and land. If the smartest capital allocator in the AI stack thinks chips are played out and power is the scarce asset, why is the market still pricing GPU makers over utilities?

items.source: Substack Notes — Yannis / The DeFi Digest
items.title: Tokenized stocks on Base are already doing $26M/24h on just $4.3M of liquidity
items.idea: 4 tokenized Base stocks are generating roughly $26M in 24-hour trading volume on Aerodrome against only about $4.3M in liquidity — a turnover ratio above 6x, pointing to either heavy speculative churn or thin-liquidity price fragility.
items.angle: That ratio is a red flag for slippage/manipulation risk in early tokenized-equity markets, but also evidence real demand exists for on-chain equity exposure before market-making infrastructure catches up.
items.tweetA: 6x turnover on $4.3M of liquidity for tokenized stocks on Base. That ratio would get you laughed out of a TradFi market-structure review. Either there's real demand for on-chain equities, or someone's about to get a very ugly slippage lesson.
items.tweetB: Tokenized equities are trading like meme coins right now — volume way outrunning liquidity. The infrastructure story here isn't 'stocks on-chain,' it's 'stocks on-chain with 1990s-emerging-market liquidity depth.' Worth watching who provides the market-making capital next.

items.title: PADD5 diesel is trading near a $210/bbl-equivalent — while Brent sits near $85
items.idea: US strikes on Iran resumed today before pausing about 2 hours later; Energy Secretary Chris Wright same-day claimed 17 million barrels flowed through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday to cap the spike. Meanwhile PADD5 diesel is near $210/bbl and NY Harbor diesel is over $200/bbl — refined-product tightness running far ahead of crude itself.
items.angle: The diesel/crude spread is the real signal, not the Brent headline. If refined products keep decoupling from crude while Hormuz stays contested, that's a crack-spread trade, not just a crude-long trade.
items.tweetA: Brent's sitting near $85. Diesel is trading like it's $210/bbl. That spread is the actual story out of Iran, not the crude headline — refiners are the trade here, not upstream. $VLO $MPC $PSX
items.tweetB: The government's own Energy Secretary is out same-day claiming 17M barrels flowed through Hormuz to talk the price down. That's the 'TACO' playbook now applied to oil — announce flow data to cap a spike. Fade the announcement, watch what diesel actually does next week.

items.title: MacroEdge: markets are in a 2000-style 'distributive phase,' held sideways to clear the OpenAI/Anthropic IPOs
items.idea: The author argues equities are being held sideways deliberately to get OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs through the pipeline, with AI-thematic enthusiasm 'dramatically cooling' from earlier in the year. He compares the pattern to the 2000 distribution phase — a slow stop rather than an abrupt end — and separately argues this month's FOMC decision barely matters because bond vigilantes are already tightening via the 10Y above 4.8%.
items.angle: If IPO issuance timing really is propping up index behavior, that's a specific, checkable calendar risk — the 'reason' for sideways markets disappears the moment OpenAI/Anthropic actually price.
items.tweetA: The bull case for staying long here isn't earnings — it's 'markets need to stay calm long enough for OpenAI and Anthropic to IPO.' That's not a valuation thesis, that's a hostage situation. What happens to index behavior the week after pricing?
items.tweetB: Bond vigilantes are doing the Fed's job for it — 10Y above 4.8% is tighter policy than anything Warsh could vote for this month. The FOMC meeting is close to irrelevant when the market's already hiking on its own.

items.title: Demand for 'AI fluency' skills is up 14x in three years — and it's leaving computer science behind
items.idea: McKinsey finds AI-fluency skill demand has risen almost 14x in three years, spreading from technical/business roles into engineering, skilled trades, and education. Meanwhile CS enrollment at US four-year schools fell more than 8% YoY even as software-developer job postings dropped — students are instead bringing AI tools into music, biology, and other majors.
items.angle: A labor-market bifurcation signal: the 'learn to code' pipeline is shrinking exactly as generalist AI-fluency demand explodes — with second-order effects on university enrollment models and which majors pay off post-2026.
items.tweetA: CS enrollment down 8%+ YoY. AI fluency demand up 14x in three years. The market isn't rewarding 'knows how to code' anymore — it's rewarding 'knows how to direct a model.' That's a full re-pricing of what a computer science degree is worth.
items.tweetB: A biology major studying AI's emulation of the brain, a music student editing tracks with AI tools — that's where the actual AI adoption curve is happening, not in CS departments. If you're modeling AI's labor impact off tech-sector hiring alone, you're missing where the volume is.

items.title: EV tax credits are gone and buyers are getting sticker shock on re-purchase
items.idea: With US EV tax credits and deep discounts disappearing, McKinsey's survey of 20,000+ consumers finds tighter budgets reshaping vehicle purchase decisions even as buyers still expect the same quality/tech/value — many EV owners are reconsidering whether their next car will be electric, hybrid, or ICE.
items.angle: A real-world test of EV demand elasticity without subsidy support — worth tracking against Tesla and legacy OEM delivery numbers over the next two quarters.
items.tweetA: The EV adoption curve was never really about the car — it was about the subsidy. Tax credits disappear, and suddenly a chunk of EV owners are reconsidering hybrid or ICE for their next purchase. Unsubsidized EV demand is about to get its first real stress test.
items.tweetB: 20,000 consumers surveyed, budgets tighter, expectations for quality/tech/value unchanged. That combination is brutal for any OEM that priced EVs assuming the credit stays permanent. Watch which automakers eat margin vs which ones lose share.

items.title: Founder-led companies hit a growth freeze right around the $1B valuation mark
items.idea: McKinsey argues AI-driven disruption and rising organizational complexity are causing many founder-led companies to freeze after crossing a $1B valuation; scaling from there to $10B+ requires refounding the business, people, and the founder personally at five distinct inflection points.
items.angle: A framework worth applying to the current AI unicorn cohort — which $1B+ AI startups show 'freeze' symptoms (slowing decision speed, org confusion) vs which are actually re-founding themselves for the next leg.
items.tweetA: McKinsey's framework: founder-led companies don't scale smoothly past $1B, they freeze — then either refound themselves or stall. With dozens of AI startups sitting exactly at that valuation mark right now, this is the filter for picking winners over the next 18 months.
items.tweetB: Everyone models startup scaling as a straight line. McKinsey's data says there are five distinct inflection points between $1B and $10B where founders have to rebuild the company and themselves. Worth asking which unicorn you're long is mid-freeze right now.

items.title: Nvidia drops $3.5B into MediaTek — its biggest direct investment outside the US
items.idea: Nvidia is buying convertible bonds as part of a $3.9B raise (Alphabet/Google also participating) to get MediaTek onto NVLink Fusion and its new NVHBM memory tech. NVHBM moves the memory controller off the AI chip into the memory stack, freeing up to 25% of chip area for compute and adding up to 30% more bandwidth at lower power. MediaTek's AI chip business is guided to ~$2B this year, targeting 15% of an $80B segment next year.
items.angle: Nvidia is buying its way into the edge/local AI layer (laptops, phones, cars) the same way it already owns the data center — a full-stack lock-in play, not just another chip deal.
items.tweetA: NVHBM frees up 25% of a chip's die area by moving the memory controller off-chip. That's not a spec bump, that's Nvidia rewriting the physics of how much compute you can pack in before the AI chip war even gets to software. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Alphabet just co-invested alongside Nvidia into MediaTek's convertible raise. When your biggest cloud customer is also funding your edge-silicon supplier, 'circular AI financing' isn't a bug in the system — it's becoming the entire capital structure of the AI stack.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman: Dong, Briggs)
items.title: AI hardware capex is $485B above 2022 levels — but only 22% of businesses have actually adopted it
items.idea: AI-related hardware investment in US national accounts is $485B above its 2022 level (annualized), about 1.5% of GDP. Taiwan's AI hardware shipments are up 76% over the same period. Yet regular business AI adoption is only 22.4% as of August, forecast to reach just 25.9% within six months. Workplace studies show 23-32% productivity gains where adopted, but broad economy-wide impact remains 'modest.'
items.angle: The capex-to-adoption gap is the single most important number in the AI trade right now — 1.5% of GDP in hardware spend against 22% business adoption is a massive bet that usage catches up to capacity.
items.tweetA: 1.5% of US GDP is now AI hardware capex. Business adoption: 22.4%. That's a 5-6x gap between what's been built and what's actually being used. Every AI infra bull case depends on that gap closing — and right now it's closing at about 3 points every six months.
items.tweetB: Taiwan AI hardware shipments +76%. US business AI adoption +3.5 points in six months. The supply side of this trade is sprinting, the demand side is jogging. That mismatch either resolves through a utilization boom or a capex hangover — there's no third option.

items.title: Tech is now officially more capital-intensive than mining — Costa says buy the miners instead
items.idea: Costa argues Big Tech's AI capex cycle has pushed the sector past traditional mining in capital intensity, while miners retain stronger margins, healthier balance sheets, and more compelling embedded growth — making miners, in his view, a more asymmetric way to express the AI investment thesis than tech itself.
items.angle: If capital intensity has actually flipped, the AI-capex trade should be expressed through the commodity/materials producers supplying the buildout, not just the hyperscalers burning the cash — worth checking against copper, uranium, and rare-earth miner valuations.
items.tweetA: Big Tech capex has gotten so heavy that mining companies now have better margins and cleaner balance sheets than the hyperscalers building AI data centers. If that's true, the asymmetric AI trade isn't Nvidia or the clouds — it's whoever's digging up what they need to build with.
items.tweetB: Capital intensity flipped: tech now spends more per dollar of revenue than mining does. Nobody prices tech stocks like extractive industries, but if the balance sheets already look like it, the multiples should start converging too.

items.title: HFIR's updated oil game plan: Iran escalating to Fujairah is back on the table
items.idea: With US strikes resuming, HFIR revisits four prior scenarios (more of the same / Iran escalates to Fujairah / Iran tries to break the naval blockade / US or Iran capitulates) across four lenses: geopolitical, fundamental, technical, positioning. Open question: will Iran tolerate the 'limited strike' playbook like it did in July (when Brent still topped $100), or escalate further this time.
items.angle: The Fujairah scenario is the one that matters for tail risk — it's the UAE's main alternate export terminal outside Hormuz, so an attack there closes off the workaround, not just the chokepoint.
items.tweetA: Iran tolerated limited US strikes in July — Brent still hit $100. The open question now is whether they tolerate round two, or escalate to Fujairah, the UAE's alternate export terminal. That's the scenario that actually breaks the 'ample flow' narrative, not another Hormuz headline.
items.tweetB: Everyone's trading Hormuz. The scenario nobody's pricing is Fujairah — the workaround terminal that makes Hormuz risk hedgeable. If that gets hit, there's no alternate route left to point to, and the whole 'flows are fine' argument disappears in a day.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Bloomberg's Frank Monkam)
items.title: Oil is up on Iran strikes, but options traders won't pay for more upside — that's the real signal
items.idea: Despite renewed US strikes and a Venezuela oil-reserve announcement, front-month oil call skew shows little demand for upside protection, and the premium on those calls keeps fading, while low-delta puts are trading richer than before the Venezuela news. Traders are treating the escalation as posturing, not a real supply shock.
items.angle: A fade-vs-fear divergence — spot is up, but derivatives positioning says smart money doesn't believe it sticks. If Hormuz flows deteriorate or refined-product stress migrates back into crude, that complacency unwinds fast.
items.tweetA: Oil's up on Iran strikes but nobody's buying calls. Skew shows puts richer than before the escalation even started. The options market is telling you this rally doesn't have real conviction behind it — which makes it exactly the kind of setup that snaps hard if Hormuz flows actually crack.
items.tweetB: The options market has seen this movie before — strikes, headline spike, no follow-through — and it's stopped paying for the sequel. That complacency is fine until the day it's wrong, and refined product prices are already signaling something the options desk hasn't priced in yet.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs)
items.title: Goldman fights the post-Jackson Hole hawkish repricing: still calls for a Fed hold in September
items.idea: Goldman forecasts August core CPI and core PCE both near 0.2% m/m, which would support a September Fed hold and pull front-end Treasury yields back down even as the market has priced in a higher probability of a Warsh hike after Jackson Hole. Goldman's payroll forecast is just 40,000 — soft, but driven by lower participation rather than layoffs.
items.angle: Goldman is explicitly betting against the market's post-Jackson Hole hawkish repricing — a contrarian call worth a position if you buy their inflation math, since front-end yields have the most room to fall if they're right.
items.tweetA: Goldman's calling BS on the market's hawkish Fed repricing since Jackson Hole. Their number: 0.2% core CPI and PCE, a 40K payroll print, and a September hold — not a hike. If they're right, front-end yields have the furthest to fall of anything in this market.
items.tweetB: 40,000 jobs added, but Goldman says it's a participation story, not a layoffs story — unemployment stays low because people are leaving the labor force, not because hiring is strong. That's a very different read on the labor market than the headline unemployment rate gives you.

items.title: Goldman: Middle East disruption is a bigger risk to diesel and European nat gas than to crude itself
items.idea: Goldman's Middle East risk framework puts more upside risk on diesel, refined products, and European natural gas than on crude oil directly — consistent with what MacroEdge and HFIR-adjacent options flow are independently flagging about PADD5 diesel trading near a $210/bbl-equivalent.
items.angle: Three separate sources this morning (Goldman, MacroEdge, and options-flow desks) are converging on the same trade: refined products and diesel are the real pressure point, not the Brent headline everyone is watching.
items.tweetA: Third source this morning saying the same thing: this isn't a crude story, it's a diesel and European nat gas story. Goldman, MacroEdge, and the options desks are all pointing at refined products while everyone else stares at the Brent number.
items.tweetB: When Goldman's macro framework and a MacroEdge trader's diesel price both point at the same crack-spread trade independently, that's not confirmation bias — that's a signal actually worth acting on before it shows up in the CPI print.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs)
items.title: Goldman just sharply raised its humanoid robot market forecasts
items.idea: Buried in the same Goldman note on Fed policy and oil, the bank disclosed it has 'sharply increased' its humanoid robot market-size forecasts, alongside staying constructive on North Asian equities and expecting further renminbi strength.
items.angle: A rates/inflation note quietly repricing an entirely different asset class (humanoid robotics) is worth flagging on its own — sell-side consensus on robotics TAM appears to be moving up meaningfully, not just AI compute.
items.tweetA: Buried inside a Fed/CPI note: Goldman just sharply raised its humanoid robot market forecast. Nobody's tweeting about that number, everyone's tweeting about the Fed. The actual market-moving revision might be the one nobody read past paragraph six.
items.tweetB: Goldman revising humanoid robot TAM upward, in the same breath as North Asian equity bullishness and renminbi strength — three separate bullish China-adjacent physical-AI calls stacked in one note. Worth pulling the actual numbers before the market catches up.

items.title: SPX sitting on 7,620-7,630 support — and September is historically the market's worst month
items.idea: SPX retested support around 7,630 and is now sitting on a support cluster at 7,620-7,630; a break lower targets 7,500 then 7,400, while resistance sits at 7,690-7,700. September is the only calendar month with a negative long-term average return for the S&P 500 and posts gains less often than any other month.
items.angle: With September's seasonal headwind lining up against a fragile support cluster, this is a level-based playbook for a buy-the-dip list rather than a reason to be outright bearish — the setup, not a forecast.
items.tweetA: SPX is sitting exactly on the one support cluster that matters — 7,620 to 7,630 — heading into the single worst-performing calendar month for US equities. Break it and the next stop is 7,500, then 7,400. Watch this level before you watch the news.
items.tweetB: September posts gains less often than any other month, and always has. That's not a reason to panic — it's a reason to have your buy-the-dip list ready before the dip happens, not after. Volatility's still suppressed, which means the dip hasn't been priced in yet.
